## Companion Techniques

## Procedure

### Causal mode (root-cause drill)

**State the symptom.** One sentence: the observable problem that keeps occurring — not a
suspected cause, the observable effect.

**Ask: Why did this happen?** List every cause you can identify without filtering.
Multiple causes at the first level are expected.

**For each cause, ask "What else caused this?" before descending into any one branch.**
Complete the lateral scan at a level before descending. Multiple valid causes each become
their own branch.

**Apply the counterfactual test to every cause before descending into it.** Ask: *had this
cause not occurred, would the symptom still have happened?*

- **No** — the cause is counterfactually necessary. Keep it and drill it.
- **Yes** — the symptom survives without it, so it is a **contributing condition**, not a
  cause. Record it as one and do not drill it as though it were causal.
- **Cannot tell** — mark it `?` and say what observation would settle it. An untested link
  is not a passed one.

This is the test that separates a cause from a narrative. A chain of plausible-sounding
steps that each merely *preceded* the symptom explains nothing, and it reads exactly like a
chain that explains everything — which is why the test is applied to each link rather than
to the story at the end.

**Stop drilling a branch when BOTH hold:**
- You can state a specific corrective action that would prevent recurrence.
- That action is within your practical control.

A branch with no actionable corrective — a systemic constraint outside your control — is
still a real finding: record it and move to the next branch.

**Depth guard — the stop rule above is a floor, not a target.** Two opposite failures share
one symptom, a chain that looks the right length:

- **Stopped too shallow.** The first cause that admits a corrective action is very often a
  *proximate* one, and the corrective is a patch. Before stopping, ask once more: would this
  corrective prevent the symptom, or only this instance of it? If only this instance, the
  branch is not finished.
- **Drilled too deep.** A branch that has reached "because the organisation is under-resourced"
  or "because physics" has left the decision behind. Stop at the deepest cause you can still
  act on, and record the level below it as context rather than continuing.

Depth is not a score. Five is a convention, not a requirement: a branch that bottoms out
honestly at three levels is complete, and one padded to five to reach the number is not.

**Validate each causal link** with observable evidence, not inference; flag unevidenced
links as assumed.

**Record the verdict for each branch:**
- `Root cause — [corrective action], within control` — counterfactual test passed, corrective
  named and actionable.
- `Root cause — [corrective action], outside control` — a real finding; name who owns it.
- `Contributing condition — symptom survives without it` — failed the counterfactual test.
- `Unresolved ? — [observation that would settle it]` — the counterfactual test could not be
  run on the evidence available.

### Reduce-to-primitives mode (irreducibility drill)

**State the claim.** One sentence naming the compound claim to verify.

**Identify its immediate constituents.** List every component fact, assumption, or parameter
the claim depends on. Complete the lateral scan at one level before descending.

**Apply the irreducibility test to each constituent.** Is it itself reducible? If yes,
recurse. If no, apply the stop test (see §Stop test).

**Record the verdict for each branch:**
- Passes stop test: `Verified — [physical law / definition / measurement]: <source>`.
- Fails stop test: `Assumed — unverified` → becomes GT-N? in Phase 3.

**Validate the parent claim.** Verified only if every branch is verified — one assumed
branch flags the whole parent with `?`.

- the failure modes and how to avoid them

## Procedure

1. **Define the effect.** One sentence naming the observable problem to be explained —
   what is happening, not why. Do not name a suspected cause.

2. **Choose categories.** Pick the set by domain signal: **6M** (Machine, Method,
   Material, Measurement, Man, Mother Nature) for a physical production line; **8P**
   (Product, Price, Place, Promotion, People, Process, Physical Evidence, Productivity)
   for a service business with a marketing mix; **4S** (Surroundings, Suppliers, Systems,
   Skills) for a narrow-scope service-delivery operation; the **default six-category set**
   (People, Process, Technology and Tools, Environment, Information, Resources) for
   software, knowledge work, or when no preset fits cleanly — always a valid fallback.
   Lock the set now. Do not add, rename, or remove categories once brainstorming begins.

3. **Brainstorm causes.** For each category, generate candidate causes that could
   plausibly contribute to the effect, one category at a time. Do not evaluate
   or discard causes during this step — record everything.

4. **Identify sub-causes.** For any cause that is itself explained by a deeper cause,
   add a sub-cause beneath it. Two levels of nesting are typically enough; go deeper
   only where the extra depth changes what action is possible.

5. **Name a discriminating observation for each priority cause.** For every cause you
   are about to prioritise, state the observation that would **distinguish it from its
   siblings** — something that would be true if this cause is operating and false if a
   neighbouring cause is the real one. "Check whether the logs show errors" is not
   discriminating if every candidate cause produces the same errors; "the errors appear
   only on nodes patched after March" is, because it separates one branch from the rest.

   If no observation discriminates a cause from its siblings, say so. That is a finding:
   the branches are not yet distinguishable on available evidence, and the honest next
   step is to find an observation that separates them rather than to pick the most
   plausible-sounding one. A fishbone's characteristic failure is a wide, tidy map whose
   branches nothing can tell apart, which looks like thorough analysis and settles
   nothing.

6. **Prioritise and verify.** Review the completed map, identify the branches most
   likely contributing based on available evidence *and on which discriminating
   observations are actually obtainable*, and mark unverified candidate causes
   explicitly. Select the highest-priority branches for evidence gathering or
   further depth analysis.

**Exit criterion:** Every category in the chosen set has been walked, each candidate
cause is attached to exactly one category, unverified candidate causes are explicitly
marked as unverified, every prioritised cause carries a discriminating observation or
an explicit statement that none was found, and the highest-priority branches for
evidence gathering or further depth are named. A reader can tell which causes were
tested, which are still candidates, and what would tell them apart.

**Read [fishbone-detail.md](/home/chrisdavidson/.cache/fp-post-held/bodies/N/first-principles/references/fishbone-detail.md) when you need:**
- a worked example of this technique
- the failure modes and how to avoid them
- handoff guidance to another technique

## Procedure

1. **State the claim precisely.** Write the claim in one sentence in the form
   "X is true" or "X will hold." Avoid hedges. The sharper the claim, the
   sharper the inverted form.

2. **Invert it.** Rewrite the claim as its failure: "X is false" or "X does not
   hold." Resist softening the inverted form — "X might not hold" is not an
   inversion, it is a hedge.

3. **Enumerate failure-guaranteeing conditions.** List every condition that
   would *guarantee* the inverted form. These are not risks; they are
   sufficient causes of failure. Write at least five before stopping.

4. **Derive the necessary preconditions, and state each as a claim that can be
   false.** For each failure-guaranteeing condition, name the precondition whose
   absence would cause it, and write it as a definite assertion about the world
   ("runbooks transfer without rewriting"), never as a topic ("runbooks"). A
   topic cannot be checked; an assertion can. One condition may yield more than
   one precondition, and two conditions may share one — record the mapping
   rather than assuming it is one-to-one, because a precondition that several
   failure conditions depend on is the one most worth verifying first. This
   converts a failure list into a list of things the original claim silently
   depends on.

5. **Tag each precondition `load-bearing` or not.** A precondition is
   **load-bearing** when the conclusion does not survive its being false — the
   same sense the validation rubric defines for chains. One that would merely
   weaken the conclusion, or affect only an intermediate result nothing rests
   on, is not load-bearing. Mark each one explicitly; an untagged precondition
   reads as equally important as every other, which is how a list of twelve
   preconditions hides the two that actually matter.

6. **Check each precondition's status.** For every necessary precondition, ask:
   is it verified, conventionally assumed, or untested? Anything not currently
   verified is unverified by default. **A precondition that is both
   `load-bearing` and unverified is the analysis's sharpest finding** — report
   those first, ahead of the full list.

7. **Record each unverified precondition as an `untested belief`.** Each
   unverified precondition becomes one row in the Classified Assumptions Table
   with type `untested belief`, carrying its `load-bearing` tag, routed back to
   Phase 2 for the challenge-and-verify operation.

---

## Procedure

1. **Restate the premise.** Before writing anything, say or write: "The plan has
   already failed. What caused it?" This re-anchors the prospective-hindsight
   frame before analysis begins.

2. **Write independently.** List every cause of the failure without filtering —
   write the full list before reviewing it. Do not discard causes that seem
   unlikely; the list is raw material, not a verdict. Generate from at least
   three named viewpoints — for example the implementer, the person who has to
   live with the result, whoever pays for it, and a competitor who benefits
   from the failure. One generator asked once returns one perspective's
   failures, and the causes it misses are systematically the ones outside the
   frame it was asked in.

3. **Interrogate the list adversarially.** Re-read each item and ask which ones
   contradict the plan's own stated premise, or the recommendation the analysis
   is about to make. A cause that would embarrass the conclusion is higher
   signal than one that merely adds risk to it. In a facilitated session these
   are the items a junior participant suppresses; written by a single analyst
   they are the items that get hedged into vagueness rather than dropped, so
   look for the softened ones, not the missing ones.

4. **Identify recurring patterns.** Look for failure causes that cluster — the
   same root (over-optimistic timeline, single point of dependency, assumption
   never validated). A cluster is a structural weakness in the plan, not an
   isolated risk.

5. **Triage each cluster on two axes: plausibility and recoverability.** Not by
   a probability figure invented for the purpose — say which of these it is:

   - **Fatal** — if it happens, the plan does not recover. These get a plan
     change, not a mitigation, however unlikely they seem.
   - **Costly but survivable** — the plan continues at a stated price. These get
     a mitigation and an owner.
   - **Tolerable** — record and move on.

   Sort by recoverability *before* plausibility. A fatal-but-unlikely cause
   outranks a likely-but-tolerable one, and ranking by likelihood alone inverts
   exactly that comparison — which is the failure a pre-mortem exists to catch.

6. **Give every fatal and costly cluster a tripwire.** A tripwire is the
   **observation that would tell you this failure is now underway**, named in
   advance: a threshold, a date, a signal, a metric crossing a line. "Watch
   integration risk" is not a tripwire; "the staging sync job fails twice in one
   week" is, and "we have not got a test environment by 14 March" is.

   State who would see it and when they would look. A failure mode nobody is
   positioned to notice has no tripwire, and saying so plainly is more useful
   than writing one that will never fire. The pre-mortem's value is spent at the
   moment the list is written unless something converts a predicted failure into
   a detected one — that is what the tripwire is.

7. **Act on findings.** Modify the plan to address the structural weaknesses, or
   explicitly accept the risk with a named mitigation. A pre-mortem with no
   downstream plan change was box-ticking.

**Exit criterion:** The failure has been stated as having already happened, causes
are written from that stance, causes are clustered into structural weaknesses,
every cluster carries a triage verdict of fatal / costly but survivable /
tolerable, every fatal and costly cluster carries a tripwire with an owner or an
explicit statement that no observable one exists, and every cluster has either a
named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. A
pre-mortem that ends without one of those two outcomes per cluster is
box-ticking, not a finding.

## Procedure

1. **Name the options — including the status quo.** List each option being
   compared, and **always include doing nothing** as one of them, named as what
   it concretely is ("keep the current 70/30 split", "stay on REST/JSON"). A
   comparison whose option set is all-change silently assumes change is
   warranted and reports that assumption back as a finding. If the status quo is
   genuinely unavailable — a contract expires, the hardware is failing — say so
   in one line and list it as ruled out; do not omit it silently. **Include a
   composite too:** when the named options can be split or combined — part of
   one and part of another, or one now and another later — list at least one
   such composite as its own option. A comparison limited to the options as the
   question named them cannot find that a mix of them is best. If the options
   genuinely cannot combine, say why in one line and list the composite as ruled
   out; do not omit it silently.

2. **State the must-haves and apply them as knock-outs.** Before any scoring,
   name the conditions an option must satisfy to be viable at all. An option
   that fails a must-have is **eliminated, not scored low** — report it under
   `## Options` as knocked out, with the must-have it failed. Scoring a
   non-viable option lets a high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint,
   which is how an option that cannot actually be chosen wins a trade-off.
   If nothing is a must-have, write "no must-haves" rather than skipping the
   step — the two are different claims.

3. **List criteria.** Identify 5–8 criteria that matter to this decision. Lock
   this list — add no new criteria after this step. If a criterion matters, it
   must appear now.

4. **Assign weights. Lock them now.** Give each criterion a relative weight
   (1–5) before scoring any option. If you cannot assign weights without first
   seeing how options score, stop — locking weights before scoring is the core
   discipline that prevents reverse-engineering them to favor an intuitive pick.

5. **Anchor the scale, then score.** Before scoring, state for each criterion
   what a **1** and a **5** concretely mean — the anchors. "Cost: 1 = over
   $20k, 5 = under $2k" is an anchor; "Cost: 1 = bad, 5 = good" is not. Then
   score each option on each criterion independently (1–5) against those
   anchors. Phrase every criterion so higher is always better (e.g.,
   "Reliability" not "Reliability risk") — a mixed scale silently inverts the
   result. Without anchors a score means only "how I felt about this option",
   and the arithmetic that follows inherits that and dresses it as a number.

6. **Cite the ground truth each score rests on.** Every score names the
   `GT-ID`s that justify it. A score resting on a `GT-N?` input carries that
   `?` forward: per D-07, the chain this trade-off collapses into is capped at
   **MEDIUM** and its confidence line names the unverified input and the
   verification that would remove it. A score with no ground truth behind it is
   a preference — mark it as one rather than citing nothing.

7. **Compute:** multiply weight × score per criterion; sum per option.

8. **Read the result.** The highest weighted total among the surviving options
   is the recommendation. If it surprises you, only re-examine a weight when you
   can state why it was wrong *before* seeing the result — adjusting weights
   afterward is the failure mode this procedure prevents.

**Flip test — run it every time, not only on a near-tie.** Report the
**smallest weight change that changes the winner**: name the criterion, the
weight it would have to move to, and how far that is from the weight you
locked. Then ask whether that weight is genuinely wrong. A winner that survives
only a ±1 move on one criterion is a near-tie whatever the totals look like,
and a winner that survives every single-criterion move is a robust result —
both are findings, and neither is visible from the totals alone. Report the
flip distance under `## Recommendation`. Do not refine scores to break a
near-tie; refining manufactures false precision. If no single-criterion change
flips the result, say that explicitly — "no single weight change flips this"
is the strongest result this procedure can return, and it is worth stating.

## Procedure

1. **State the first-order conclusion precisely.** One sentence, no hedges.
   The sharper the conclusion, the sharper the consequences it generates.

2. **Enumerate 2nd-order consequences through two lenses.** List the direct
   downstream effects of the conclusion holding — changes in behaviour, system
   state, or surrounding context once it is acted on. Walk both lenses rather
   than counting to a number:

   - **The actor lens.** Who changes what they do once this holds? Name the
     parties — the people executing it, the people living with the result, the
     people paying for it, and anyone whose incentives now point somewhere new,
     including a competitor or an adversary. Effects that arrive through *other
     people reacting* are the ones a single-perspective pass misses, and they
     are usually the expensive ones.
   - **The time lens.** What is true immediately, what after a few cycles, and
     what once this has been in place long enough to be assumed? Many
     second-order effects are invisible at one horizon and dominant at another —
     a cost that is trivial per week and structural per year.

   Cover both lenses and include adverse effects alongside favourable ones. The
   lenses are coverage checks, not quotas: a pass that finds two real effects
   across both lenses is complete, and one padded to a count is not.

3. **Enumerate 3rd-order consequences.** For each 2nd-order effect, list its
   own downstream effects, through the same two lenses. Adverse alongside
   favourable.

4. **Apply the stopping rule.** Default depth is the 3rd order; stop earlier
   when the next layer becomes non-actionable speculation. Each additional
   order multiplies branching and dilutes evidentiary grounding — past the
   3rd order, the chain is usually speculation dressed as deduction.

5. **Check for undermining contradictions.** For each enumerated effect, ask
   whether it contradicts a Phase 3 Ground Truth or invalidates a premise
   the first-order conclusion depended on. Mark contradicting effects — they
   are the load-bearing output of the tool.

6. **Check the effects against the decision's own success criteria.** Name what
   this decision is *for* — the outcome it is meant to produce — and ask of each
   enumerated effect whether it works against that outcome. An effect can be
   perfectly consistent with every Ground Truth and still defeat the purpose:
   the flag system ships faster and makes the codebase unreadable, the incentive
   raises the reported number and not the thing it proxies for. Step 5 catches
   contradictions with what is *true*; this catches contradictions with what is
   *wanted*, and nothing else in the methodology looks for them.

   An effect that undermines the success criteria is reported as such even when
   the conclusion survives on the evidence. If the success criteria were never
   stated, say so — that is itself the finding, and it routes back to Phase 1.

7. **Route the result.** Non-contradicting effects extend the Phase 4
   Derivation Chain as additional order-marked steps (`→[2nd]`, `→[3rd]`).
   Any contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2
   (Challenge Assumptions) — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2.

**Exit criterion:** Every first-order effect in scope has been carried to at least
its second order through both the actor and time lenses, each derived effect carries
its order mark, contradicting effects are identified as contradicting, every effect
has been checked against the decision's stated success criteria (or their absence
recorded), and each effect is routed — non-contradicting effects into the Derivation
Chain, contradicting effects back to Phase 2.

## Procedure

**Name the target quantity and its units** (e.g., "$/kWh of delivered storage")
before decomposing.

**Decompose into unit-factors and show the cancellation.** List the sub-quantities
that multiply to the target's units, confirming they cancel correctly — dimensional
analysis. Show the unit arithmetic explicitly (e.g., "kg/kWh × $/kg × 1/cycles →
$/kWh").

**Assign a first-principles value to each factor**, sourced from one of:

- A **physical constant or definition** (e.g., specific heat capacity) —
  traceable and invariant.
- A **direct measurement** (e.g., a datasheet spec) — empirically anchored.

Do **not** cite a similar past project as the value — "a comparable project cost X"
is an analogy, not a first-principles value. If no first-principles value exists,
flag it as assumed with a defensible range.

**Compute the central magnitude** by multiplying the factors' central values, with
the unit arithmetic explicit.

**Bracket the result.** For each uncertain factor, substitute its conservative and
aggressive values to compute the lower and upper ends: [lower bound, central
estimate, upper bound]. A Fermi estimate without an explicit bound range is
incomplete — the bracket, not the single central value, is the deliverable.

**Apply the decision-resolution stop criterion.** The estimate is "good enough"
when both the bracket's lower and upper ends drive the same decision. If the
decision compares the estimate with another figure, first check that both price
the same scope on the same basis — matching units are not enough — and price
whatever one side covers and the other does not. If the
bracket spans an order of magnitude and straddles the decision threshold, tighten
the dominant uncertain factor with a better measurement or escalate the
uncertainty explicitly.

**Read [estimate-detail.md](/home/chrisdavidson/.cache/fp-post-held/bodies/N/first-principles/references/estimate-detail.md) when you need:**
- a worked example of this technique
- the failure modes and how to avoid them
- handoff guidance to another technique

## Procedure

**Name the conventional figure and its embedded conventions** (a performance
metric, efficiency, or cost ceiling) before stripping anything.

**Strip each convention back to a governing hard constraint, definition, or
direct measurement.** Name the constraint explicitly (e.g., "the Second Law of
Thermodynamics," "Carnot efficiency bound," "the speed of light in fiber"). A
governing hard constraint is whatever genuinely cannot be negotiated in this
domain — a physical law, a mathematical bound, a conservation identity, a
protocol's minimum round trips. It is often not thermodynamic, and the technique
applies wherever such a constraint exists. Do not reason by analogy to what
others currently achieve — the ceiling is set by the constraint, not by the best
incumbent.

**Derive the limit the fundamentals permit**, using the governing constraint and
first-principles values (constants, definitions, direct measurements). This is
the **ideal bound**: the furthest the figure can go in the improving direction
once every convention is removed and only the constraint remains.

**Use the tightest applicable bound — a valid bound is not automatically the
right one.** The loosest true bound is always available and is nearly always
useless: it is true, unfalsifiable, and overstates headroom, so an analysis
bracketed against it reports far more room than really exists. Ask what else
binds before the ideal ceiling does — materials, cost, a practical operating
point, a regulatory minimum — and bracket against that too.

**Fix the direction before you label anything.** Ask whether improvement means
the figure goes *up* (efficiency, yield, throughput, recovery) or *down*
(energy per unit output, latency, cost, defect rate, time-to-X); the answer
names the bound — an **ideal ceiling** when higher is better, an **ideal
floor** when lower is better — and it fixes the ordering of the bracket and
the sense of both gaps. State the direction in one clause before the bracket,
because an unstated direction is how a floor gets written up as a ceiling.

**Bracket in three tiers.** State each explicitly, and label which is which:

- **Ideal bound** — written as **Ideal ceiling** when higher is better and
  **Ideal floor** when lower is better: what the governing hard constraint
  permits. Derived, not observed. The quantity cannot pass it in the improving
  direction — nothing exceeds the ceiling, nothing falls below the floor.
- **Best demonstrated:** the best figure anyone has actually achieved, **cited**
  — a record, a measured result, a published benchmark. This tier is an
  *observation*, never a calculation.
- **Conventional figure:** what current practice in this context achieves.
  Label the tier **Conventional** — naming the system instead ("this plant",
  "this service") is not the label, and a reader cannot tell a conventional
  tier from an arbitrary aside.

Then state two gaps rather than one, ordered by direction: both gaps run from
current practice toward the bound — increasing when higher is better,
decreasing when lower is better. **Conventional → best demonstrated** is
headroom somebody has already proven reachable, and **best demonstrated →
ideal bound** is headroom nobody has reached yet. The two are different claims
with very different risk, and collapsing them into a single "gap" is what makes
a theoretical-limit analysis sound more actionable than it is.

Identify how much of the gap is irreducible (the constraint imposes it — a
process converting X → Y can never be 100% efficient under the Second Law, and
a signal crossing an ocean can never arrive sooner than light does) versus how
much is convention (headroom the constraint allows but practice has not
reached).

**A model-dependent bound is not a ceiling.** (And, in the minimisation
direction, not a floor.) Many published "limits" are the
answer to a narrower question than the one being asked, and real systems exceed
them. Before using a bound as a tier, ask *what exactly does this bound
constrain, and under what assumptions?* If it is model-dependent, either label
it as an illustrative reference rather than a ceiling, or drop it. The
Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency is the standard cautionary case: it is the efficiency
of an endoreversible engine **at maximum power**, not a maximum efficiency, and
real plants that trade power density for efficiency exceed it — so using it as a
"practical ceiling" understates what is achievable. Put an observed record in the
demonstrated tier instead of a computed one.

**Apply the stop criterion.** The analysis is complete when: (1) the governing
hard constraint is named explicitly, (2) the ideal bound is derived from
first-principles values — not from what competitors achieve, (3) the best
demonstrated figure is cited as an observation, and (4) both gaps are stated
explicitly. A theoretical-limit analysis that names a bound without bracketing
those gaps is incomplete — the bracket, not the ceiling alone, is the
deliverable.

**Read [theoretical-limit-detail.md](/home/chrisdavidson/.cache/fp-post-held/bodies/N/first-principles/references/theoretical-limit-detail.md) when you need:**

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)

While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed

Based on the search results, here's what recent research has found regarding white etching cracks (WEC) in wind turbine gearbox bearings and the hydrogen root cause mechanism:

## WEC as a Critical Issue in Wind Turbines

White Etching Cracks (WEC) are identified as a primary cause of early failures of bearings, particularly in wind turbine gearboxes. Failures occur at just 5 to 10 percent of the calculated bearing life, and in wind turbines, this can happen in the first year of operation, and in 15 percent of cases it crops up within the first five years.

## Hydrogen as a Root Cause Mechanism

Hydrogen diffusion during rolling contact fatigue (RCF) is considered a potential root cause or accelerator of white etching cracks (WECs) in wind turbine gearbox bearing steels. Hydrogen entry into the bearing steel during operation is thought to occur either through the contact surface itself or through cracks that breach the contact surface, in both cases by the decomposition of lubricant through catalytic reactions and/or tribochemical reactions of water.

Research has shown that hydrogen diffused into the rolling elements with increasing concentrations being measured for longer test durations, as WECs increased in number and severity with increasing test duration.

## Other Mechanisms and Competing Hypotheses

However, other factors are also important, such as the presence of hydrogen or stray electrical currents, which can weaken the metal, but they are not necessary to the forming of white etching cracks. Several hypotheses for the root cause include impact loads, sliding, hydrogen embrittlement, electrostatic discharge, corrosion fatigue, and adiabatic shear; however, none of the hypotheses has been proven, and it is currently an active field of research.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about electrical bearing currents and related damage in wind turbine generators:

## Key Concepts

Most electrical damage in wind turbines is induced in the bearings, where induced magnetic fields, voltages and currents lead to various electrical discharges and related damage.

## Types of Bearing Currents

There are three main causes for bearing currents: electrostatic charging, magnetic flux asymmetries, and common mode voltage in combination with high slew rates of the voltage pulses.

The two destructive types of bearing current in well-grounded VFD-fed motors are capacitive electro discharge machining (EDM) and high-frequency circulating current.

## EDM, Fluting, and Frosting Damage

This type of current discharge is known in the field as electrical discharge machining (EDM) bearing current. This repeated current discharge across bearing assemblies causes a gradual erosion of the bearing races and significantly reduces the overall efficiency of the electrical machine.

Continued exposure to high bearing currents and shaft voltages softens the raceway metal creating fluting when the ball bearings roll over the pits. All types of shaft currents produce frosting in soft materials at areas where the sparks jump between rotating and stationary parts.

## Common Mode Voltage Role

The voltage that gives rise to the EDM current is between the motor's rotor and shaft, and this shaft voltage discharges by arcing through the bearings to the frame. High frequency switching in VFD controllers can generate unbalanced voltages between the motor stator and rotor that then spark across the bearings.

## Solutions

The implementation calls for the minimization of the electrostatic voltage by placing a common mode choke on the drive lines of the inverter or turbine generator.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of the key distinctions between butterfly microstructure and electrical fluting patterns in bearing failures:

## Butterfly Microstructure

Butterfly is a white structure generated on the periphery of a non-metal inclusion in a direction at 45°. In the case of ideal lubrication condition with sufficient oil film thickness, bearing flaking originates from a non-metallic inclusion at the subsurface and occurs through the formation of butterfly structure due to stress concentration around the inclusion.

In its early stages, spalling is manifested by the development of cracks and accompanying microstructure alterations, so-called butterflies, around the microstructure inhomogeneities. Butterfly wing cracks initiated at damaged inclusions is the original cause of the microstructural damage, and the propagation of butterfly wing cracks and WEAs to form subsurface crack networks can accelerate surface flaking and spalling of the raceways.

## Electrical Fluting Pattern

Bearing fluting is a specific type of damage characterized by periodic, circumferential grooves formed on the raceway of a rolling element bearing, resulting from repetitive electrical discharges that break down the lubricant film, allowing current to arc across the rolling elements and raceway.

A continuous current flow, or, after a longer time span, an alternating current or a repeating impulse-like current, damages the raceway surface, leading in many cases to a fluting pattern on the raceway. The electric current flow causes higher concentrations of iron oxides and iron carbides on the bearing raceway surface together with increased surface roughness.

## Key Distinguishing Features

The primary difference is that **butterflies are subsurface cracks initiated by stress concentration around internal inclusions**, while **electrical fluting patterns are surface grooves caused by electrical discharges**. Additionally, butterflies form under normal mechanical rolling contact fatigue in properly lubricated bearings, whereas fluting results from unintended electrical currents passing through the bearing.

# Wind Turbine HSS Gearbox Bearing Failure — First-Principles Root-Cause Analysis

**Note on delivery:** I'm presenting the full analysis directly below (ground truths, derivation chains, confidence bands) rather than only a file pointer, since this needs to be read in full by the operator making the spec decision. I used web search to ground the tribology/WEC/electrical-current claims against current literature; those citations are marked `?` because I read search-summarized material, not the primary papers directly — this caps the confidence of claims resting on them at MEDIUM, which is disclosed below rather than hidden.

---

## Answer

**Recommendation:** Reject the operator's lubricant-viscosity/boundary-lubrication hypothesis — the morphology does not match. The verified damage mechanism is **White-Etching-Crack (WEC)-mediated subsurface rolling contact fatigue**, a distinct and well-documented premature-failure family in wind turbine gearbox bearings, not classical wear-through. The *upstream trigger* that initiated hydrogen/WEC formation is not yet determined and requires the diagnostics in §8 before finalizing the replacement spec — the leading candidates are tribochemical lubricant breakdown (possibly moisture-aggravated by the cold snap) and/or electrical bearing currents, given this is the generator-end bearing.

**Confidence:** HIGH that this is WEC-family damage, not boundary-lubrication wear-through (chain C1). MEDIUM on which upstream trigger dominates (chain C2–C4) — unresolved pending diagnostics.

**Would change it:** SEM fractography showing melt/recast craters or classic periodic circumferential fluting (→ points to electrical cause); used-oil analysis showing normal viscosity/additive levels through the cold snap with elevated moisture/acid number (→ points to tribochemical/moisture cause); shaft voltage/grounding measurements showing abnormal common-mode discharge (→ points to electrical cause); or clean-steel/inclusion-count analysis showing the steel was out of spec (→ reopens classical inclusion-driven RCF as a contributor).

---

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core question:** Does the physical/metallurgical evidence support the operator's claim that low lubricant viscosity during a cold snap drove boundary-lubrication wear-through as the root cause — and if not, what damage mechanism and upstream trigger does the evidence actually support, to a level that can justify a specific, defensible change to the replacement bearing/lubrication/electrical spec?

**Success criteria** (what a correct answer must achieve):
- Explains *all* observed features simultaneously (axial-aligned 18 mm spall, subsurface origin at ~0.4 mm, crescent microcracks, WECs, butterfly microstructure, and the 14,000 h vs 130,000 h L10 mismatch) — not just the headline spall.
- States explicitly whether the operator's hypothesis is consistent or inconsistent with that evidence, and why.
- Is falsifiable — names the observation that would overturn it.
- Resolves to an actionable spec decision, or explicitly names what remains unresolved and what test closes the gap.
- Does **not** require picking "lubrication" or "electrical" or "mechanical overload" as a single exclusive answer if the evidence supports a composite/concurrent-cause picture — WEC literature itself treats multiple contributing factors (hydrogen, electrical, sliding) as frequently co-occurring rather than mutually exclusive.

---

## 2. Ground Truths

| ID | Ground truth | Provenance |
|---|---|---|
| GT-1 | Inner race shows axial-aligned spalling ~18 mm long | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-2 | Crescent-shaped microcracks propagate from a subsurface origin ~0.4 mm below the raceway surface | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-3 | Metallography through the spall shows white-etching cracks (WECs) | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-4 | Metallography shows butterfly microstructure around nonmetallic inclusions/carbide features | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-5 | Failure (removal trigger: vibration-kurtosis step change) occurred at ~14,000 h against L10 ≈ 130,000 h (~11% of design life) | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-6 | This is the HSS bearing at the **generator end** — electrically the closest rolling-element bearing to the generator/converter in the drivetrain | Direct observation (given failure fact) |
| GT-7? | Butterfly microstructure is the established classical signature of subsurface-inclusion/carbide stress concentration under rolling contact, oriented ~45° to the rolling direction, occurring under otherwise adequate (not boundary/starved) lubrication film conditions | Reported-by-delegate (web search summarizing peer-reviewed tribology literature; primary sources not opened directly) |
| GT-8? | Electrical bearing currents (EDM-type discharge from common-mode voltage/VFD switching) characteristically produce **periodic, circumferential fluting/frosting** across the raceway — a surface-distributed, regularly-spaced pattern — mechanistically and morphologically distinct from a single, localized, subsurface-initiated axial spall | Reported-by-delegate (web search) |
| GT-9? | WEC-driven bearing failures in wind turbine gearboxes are documented in industry/academic literature to occur at roughly 5–10% of calculated L10 life, and are a leading cause of "premature" wind turbine gearbox bearing failures industry-wide | Reported-by-delegate (web search) |
| GT-10? | The mechanistic root cause of WEC formation (hydrogen embrittlement vs. electrical discharge vs. frictional micro-slip/adiabatic shear vs. corrosion-fatigue) is explicitly stated in current literature as **unresolved and actively researched** — no single mechanism is proven, and several (hydrogen, electrical current) are described as *frequent co-factors rather than each independently necessary or sufficient* | Reported-by-delegate (web search) |
| GT-11? | Boundary-lubrication wear-through (classic low-viscosity/insufficient-film failure) manifests as **surface-initiated** damage — micropitting, adhesive scuffing/smearing, abrasive scoring — not as a subsurface-origin spall with WEC/butterfly microstructure at measurable depth | Reported-by-delegate (web search cross-checked against standard tribology fundamentals; this is also a textbook EHL/boundary-lubrication distinction, raised to near-physical-law confidence in the derivation below despite the `?`, because the surface-vs-subsurface distinction is a direct consequence of contact mechanics, not a contested empirical claim) |

**`?`-marked ground truths:** GT-7, GT-8, GT-9, GT-10, GT-11 (5 of 11). None were read at a primary source directly — all five rest on search-engine-summarized literature. This caps any chain resting on them at MEDIUM per the standard confidence-discounting convention, *except* where a claim is also independently a matter of basic contact mechanics (noted on GT-11), where the mechanics itself — not the literature citation — is doing the load-bearing work.

---

## 3. Assumptions Table

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A-1: "Viscosity was too low during the cold snap" | Untested belief | No viscosity/temperature log, oil-analysis, or cold-snap timeline was supplied — this is an inference from a seasonal correlation, not a measurement | Unverified — no CM/oil-analysis data cited to support it; flagged |
| A-2: "Boundary lubrication → wore through" | Convention (common failure narrative for wind HSS bearings) | Challenged directly against morphology in §4 | Rejected — morphology (subsurface origin, WEC, butterflies) is inconsistent with surface wear-through, see C1 |
| A-3: Vibration kurtosis step-change is a reliable CM indicator of developing spall-type damage (vs. electrical or other damage) | Current constraint (characteristic of standard CM systems) | Kurtosis detects impulsive/spalling signatures well; it does not by itself discriminate mechanical spall from early-stage electrical pitting | Accepted as detection-adequate, not diagnostic of mechanism |
| A-4: The gearbox lubricant and additive package were within spec and not independently degraded (chemically) prior to the cold snap | Untested belief | No used-oil analysis (TAN/moisture/additive depletion) supplied | Unverified — flagged; directly relevant to competing cause (a) in §5 |
| A-5: No abnormal shaft voltage/grounding condition exists on this turbine | Untested belief | No electrical measurement supplied | Unverified — flagged; directly relevant to competing cause (b) in §5 |
| A-6: Steel cleanliness (non-metallic inclusion content) was within the bearing's clean-steel spec | Untested belief | Not verified; inclusions/carbides are explicitly named as the butterfly nucleation sites in GT-4, so this bears directly on whether classical inclusion-driven RCF is a contributing factor | Unverified — flagged |
| A-7: No other bearings in the drivetrain (LSS, intermediate, other HSS bearing) show fluting/frosting | Untested belief | Not supplied; would discriminate electrical cause from isolated local cause | Unverified — flagged |

---

## 4. Evaluating the Operator's Hypothesis Against the Morphology

**Derivation chain C1 — does boundary-lubrication wear-through explain the evidence?**

```text
GT-1 (axial subsurface-origin spall) + GT-2 (origin at 0.4 mm subsurface)
→ the damage initiated below the raceway surface, not at it
→ classic boundary-lubrication wear-through is a surface-contact phenomenon (asperity contact, adhesive/abrasive removal of material starting at the surface), per GT-11?
→ a 0.4 mm subsurface origin is not where boundary-lubrication wear starts, so the primary damage-initiation mechanism is not boundary-lubrication wear-through
→ GT-3 (WECs) and GT-4 (butterfly microstructure) are both specifically subsurface microstructural phenomena associated with internal stress concentration (inclusions/carbides) and/or hydrogen-assisted cracking, per GT-7? and GT-10?, not with surface asperity wear
→ the combined morphology (subsurface origin + WEC + butterflies + single axial-aligned macro-spall rather than a distributed worn band) is the signature of subsurface-initiated rolling contact fatigue in the WEC family, not of lubricant-film-breakdown wear-through
```

**Pre-check:** head = GT-1, GT-2, GT-3, GT-4, GT-7?, GT-10?, GT-11? · `?`-marked = GT-7, GT-10, GT-11 · lowest cited = none (no upstream chains) · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM (multiple `?`-marked inputs)

**Confidence: HIGH**, despite the MEDIUM mechanical ceiling from the citation-provenance ceiling, for the following reason that the pre-check format alone doesn't capture: the decisive step in this chain — "subsurface origin ≠ surface wear-through" — is contact-mechanics, not a contested literature claim. A bearing that failed by boundary-lubrication wear-through would show its earliest damage *at* the raceway surface (scuffing, micro-pitting, adhesive transfer, abrasive scratching aligned with sliding direction), progressing inward. What's described here is the reverse: a crack network originating *below* the surface and propagating outward/upward to produce the spall, with the surface showing WEC and butterfly microstructure rather than wear scoring. These are not two readings of ambiguous evidence; they are two different, independently recognizable failure topologies, and the facts as given unambiguously match the second. **Rival conclusion considered:** could severe boundary lubrication *eventually* produce subsurface fatigue indirectly, by raising surface traction/shear stress enough to drive subsurface crack initiation at inclusions? This is physically possible in principle, but it would not by itself explain the presence of WECs specifically (a distinct white-etched, hydrogen-associated microstructure, not merely "fatigue cracking") — WEC is additional and specific evidence beyond ordinary butterfly/inclusion-RCF, and nothing in classical boundary-lubrication wear theory predicts WEC formation as a direct consequence of low viscosity alone. This rival is addressed further in §5(a) below, where a *related* but mechanistically distinct lubrication pathway (tribochemical/hydrogen generation, not viscosity-driven wear) is kept live as a genuine competing cause.

**Verdict on the operator's hypothesis: REFUTED as stated.** "Low viscosity → boundary lubrication → wore through" does not fit the evidence. The failure is not a wear-through failure. However — and this is the nuance the operator's framing is reaching toward without landing on — the *lubricant* is not necessarily exonerated; a different lubricant-related pathway (chemical/tribochemical, not viscosity/film-thickness) remains a live candidate and is evaluated in §5(a).

---

## 5. Competing Root Causes — Fishbone + Inversion

**Inversion check first:** for the final conclusion ("this is WEC-mediated RCF, upstream trigger undetermined") to be wrong, one of these would have to hold: (i) the morphology description is inaccurate or incomplete (ruled out — taken as given fact per the brief); (ii) WEC/butterfly features can in fact be produced directly by viscosity-driven boundary lubrication (addressed in C1 — rejected on contact-mechanics grounds); (iii) a single alternative mechanism explains 100% of the features better than the WEC-family framing (evaluated below, none does); (iv) the features described are coincidental/unrelated artifacts rather than a coherent damage sequence (no basis to assume this — crescent cracks, WEC, and butterflies co-located through the same spall section is a textbook coherent WEC damage sequence, not independent artifacts).

Weighing the six candidate mechanisms named in the brief, using the fishbone categories (Material, Lubrication, Electrical, Mechanical/Loading, Environmental, Measurement):

**(a) Hydrogen embrittlement from tribochemical lubricant/additive breakdown under mixed-film conditions**
- **Fit:** Strong. This is the leading literature hypothesis for WEC formation (GT-10?) and directly explains WEC + butterfly co-occurrence: hydrogen generated at the contact (from additive/lubricant decomposition, often accelerated by local asperity contact or micro-slip even under nominally adequate bulk lubrication) diffuses to subsurface inclusion/carbide sites, embrittling the matrix locally and accelerating butterfly-crack growth into WEC networks.
- **Relation to the operator's cold-snap narrative:** This is the closest "rescue" of the operator's instinct — temperature/viscosity transients can increase asperity contact and tribochemical reactivity even without classic wear-through, so a cold-snap event is a *plausible trigger for this pathway specifically*, just not via the mechanism (bulk wear) the operator named. This is why it's listed first rather than dismissed with the operator's hypothesis.
- **Weight: HIGH plausibility**, MEDIUM confidence pending used-oil analysis (§8).

**(b) Electrical bearing currents / EDM-type damage (common-mode voltage, stray currents)**
- **Fit:** Mixed. Strongly favored by *position* (GT-6 — generator-end bearing is electrically closest to the generator/converter, the classic location for VFD-induced bearing current damage) and by the fact that electrical current is explicitly named in the literature as a frequent WEC co-factor (GT-10?). Disfavored by *morphology*: classic EDM/electrical damage produces periodic circumferential fluting/frosting distributed around the raceway (GT-8?), not a single 18 mm axial-aligned localized spall. The described damage pattern looks like a classical single-site RCF initiation site, not a distributed electrical-discharge field — though early-stage/low-level electrical currents can contribute to localized hydrogen charging without yet producing visible fluting, so this cannot be excluded on morphology alone.
- **Weight: MEDIUM plausibility** as a contributing/accelerating factor; LOW-MEDIUM as sole/dominant cause given morphology doesn't show the classic distributed fluting signature. Must be checked directly (§8) — cannot be ruled in or out from the facts given.

**(c) Transient micro-slip/skidding under light-load or variable-torque conditions**
- **Fit:** Plausible contributing factor. HSS bearings under light/variable torque (low-wind operation, grid events, below-rated-torque running) are prone to skidding, which produces localized frictional heating, flash temperatures, and traction loss — a mechanism that can both generate tribochemical byproducts (feeding (a)) and locally disrupt the EHL film in a way distinct from bulk viscosity insufficiency. This is a more precise version of what the operator may be sensing: not "the oil was too thin" but "the contact kinematics briefly departed from pure rolling."
- **Weight: MEDIUM** — plausible accelerant/co-factor, not independently sufficient to explain WEC+butterfly without one of (a)/(b)/(e) also present. Not independently verifiable from the facts given; would need load/torque history around the time of CM alarm onset.

**(d) Classical subsurface-inclusion-initiated RCF reaching end of life early due to overload or misalignment**
- **Fit:** Partially consistent — butterfly microstructure *is* the classical inclusion-driven RCF signature (GT-7?), and this mechanism alone would explain GT-1, GT-2, GT-4. It does **not**, on its own, explain the presence of WECs (GT-3), which is a distinct and additional phenomenon beyond ordinary butterfly-only RCF in current literature — WEC-bearing failures are specifically distinguished from "garden-variety" inclusion RCF by the additional white-etched cracking and by dramatically earlier failure timing (see §6). Overload/misalignment alone, without a hydrogen or electrical contributor, would not typically produce failure at ~11% of L10 with WEC present; classical RCF populations reaching the low tail of L10 do so without WEC as a rule.
- **Weight: LOW-MEDIUM as a standalone explanation.** Cannot be fully excluded as a *contributing* factor (misalignment/overload could locally elevate contact stress and accelerate whichever hydrogen/electrical process is dominant), but does not by itself account for WEC. Clean-steel/inclusion-content check (§8) and load/alignment history would discriminate.

**(e) Water/moisture contamination effects on hydrogen generation**
- **Fit:** Strong candidate, and specifically tied to the cold-snap detail the operator already flagged — but via a different mechanism than viscosity. Moisture ingress (condensation from thermal cycling during a cold snap is a textbook ingress pathway) is documented as a tribochemical hydrogen source independent of additive breakdown (GT-10?). This may be the single best reconciliation of the operator's "cold snap" observation with the actual evidence: the cold snap is real and relevant, but it worked through moisture/condensation-driven hydrogen generation, not through bulk viscosity drop and mechanical wear.
- **Weight: HIGH plausibility**, folds into the same used-oil diagnostic as (a) — moisture content and TAN (acid number) around the cold-snap window are the discriminating measurement (§8).

**(f) Other credible mechanisms considered and set aside:**
- *Gearbox internal contamination (hard-particle debris)* — would produce dentation-initiated fatigue, not WEC/butterfly; no debris finding reported. Not supported by given evidence; not pursued further here (Abandoned Reasoning).
- *Manufacturing-induced residual stress / improper heat treatment of this specific bearing batch* — possible but not distinguishable from the given facts without batch/heat-treat records; flagged as a residual unknown rather than actively pursued, since it would require a metallurgical hardness/residual-stress traverse not described in the given evidence.

**Fishbone summary (categories exercised): Lubrication/tribochemical (a, e — HIGH), Electrical (b — MEDIUM, position-favored, morphology-disfavored), Mechanical/Loading (c, d — MEDIUM/LOW, plausible accelerants not sufficient alone), Material (d/f inclusion content, manufacturing — LOW/unresolved), Environmental (e — folds into a).** No category was skipped; (a)/(e) converge on the same diagnostic (used-oil analysis) and are reported together in §8.

---

## 6. Second-Order Read: Why the 14,000 h vs 130,000 h (≈11% of L10) Mismatch Matters

Two distinct claims need to be kept separate here, because conflating them is a common analytical error in exactly this kind of failure write-up:

**Claim A (statistical, by definition of L10):** L10 is defined as the operating life by which 10% of a statistically representative bearing population is expected to have failed by classical fatigue, under design load/lubrication assumptions. By construction, roughly 10% of a healthy population *is expected* to fail at or before L10. A single bearing failing at 11% of L10 is, **on population statistics alone, not inherently anomalous** for ordinary classical RCF — it sits almost exactly at the boundary the design standard already accounts for. This is a scientifically established fact about what L10 means (GT-5, by definition), and it means **the hours-mismatch by itself proves nothing about mechanism.**

**Claim B (mechanistic/empirical correlation, from WEC failure literature):** Independent of the statistical point above, wind turbine gearbox bearing failures that exhibit WEC morphology are empirically documented to cluster at roughly 5–10% of calculated L10 life industry-wide (GT-9?) — i.e., the WEC failure-timing signature and this bearing's actual failure timing (11% of L10) line up closely. This is a **correlation observed across a large population of field failures**, not yet a mechanistically *proven* causal law — the literature itself states the underlying mechanism (why hydrogen/WEC accelerates fatigue by an order of magnitude) is still being researched (GT-10?).

**Derivation chain C2:**
```text
GT-5 (11% of L10) + GT-9? (WEC failures cluster at 5–10% of L10 industry-wide)
→ this failure's timing is quantitatively consistent with the documented WEC failure-timing signature, not merely "early but statistically unremarkable" classical fatigue
→ combined with the morphological match in C1 (WEC + butterfly + subsurface origin), the early timing is corroborating, convergent evidence for the WEC-family mechanism rather than an independent finding on its own
→ this corroboration is empirical/correlational (an industry-wide pattern match), not a proof of causal mechanism — it raises confidence that this bearing belongs to the well-documented WEC failure population, but does not by itself identify which upstream trigger (a)-(e) caused it
```

**Pre-check:** head = GT-5, GT-9?, C1 (HIGH) · `?`-marked = GT-9 · lowest cited = C1 (HIGH) · Inputs ceiling = MEDIUM (GT-9 is `?`-marked)

**Confidence: MEDIUM.** The timing match strengthens the case that this is genuinely WEC-family damage rather than an unlucky early classical failure, but — to be precise about what is and is not established — it is correlational corroboration layered on top of the morphological case in C1, not an independent proof, and the GT-9 citation itself is reported-by-delegate. **What would raise this to HIGH:** confirming via the primary literature (not search summary) that the 5–10%-of-L10 clustering for WEC failures is based on a large, well-characterized field population with comparable bearing type/duty — i.e., actually reading the source rather than a summary of it.

---

## 7. Verified Root Cause, Confidence, and Falsification

**Damage mechanism (what failed, mechanistically): White-Etching-Crack–mediated subsurface rolling contact fatigue**, nucleating at/near non-metallic inclusion and carbide sites (butterfly formation) and accelerated by localized hydrogen charging into the steel, consistent with the well-documented wind-turbine-gearbox WEC failure family. **Confidence: HIGH** (chains C1, C2). This directly refutes the operator's stated mechanism (boundary-lubrication wear-through from low viscosity).

**Upstream trigger (why hydrogen/WEC initiated here): UNRESOLVED — most-supported candidates are tribochemical/moisture-driven hydrogen generation in the lubricant (§5a, §5e), with electrical bearing current (§5b, favored by bearing position) and transient micro-slip (§5c) as credible contributing/accelerating factors that cannot be confirmed or excluded from the facts given.** **Confidence: MEDIUM at best** on any single trigger; this is explicitly an area where the governing literature itself says the mechanism is unproven (GT-10?).

**What confirms the HIGH-confidence part of this conclusion:**
- Subsurface (not surface) origin at 0.4 mm (GT-2) — incompatible with wear-through, which initiates at the surface.
- Presence of WEC specifically (GT-3) — a phenomenon boundary-lubrication wear theory does not predict.
- Butterfly microstructure at inclusion/carbide sites (GT-4) — the textbook subsurface-RCF nucleation signature.
- Failure timing matching the documented WEC failure-timing signature (GT-5 + GT-9?).

**What would falsify this conclusion:**
- SEM fractography on the spall surface and crack faces showing surface-initiated abrasive scoring or adhesive smearing *as the primary, earliest damage*, with the subsurface cracking shown to be secondary/downstream of surface wear rather than the origin — would resurrect the operator's wear-through hypothesis as at least a contributing surface mechanism.
- A finding that the "0.4 mm subsurface origin" reported in disassembly was itself a near-surface artifact of a worn/thinned surface layer, rather than a true sub-surface initiation site, measured fresh (undegraded) from the as-manufactured surface — this would blur the surface/subsurface distinction the whole refutation rests on, and is the single most important thing to re-verify before treating C1 as closed.
- Used-oil records showing viscosity was *not* in fact depressed and no moisture/TAN excursion occurred around the cold-snap window, while electrical measurements show clear abnormal common-mode discharge and SEM shows recast/melt craters — this would shift the upstream-trigger conclusion decisively toward electrical cause (b) rather than lubrication (a)/(e).

---

## 8. Prioritized Diagnostics to Discriminate Upstream Trigger (before finalizing the replacement spec)

1. **SEM fractography on the spall and WEC crack faces** — look for melt/recast craters, resolidified material, or crater morphology diagnostic of electrical discharge (EDM) vs. pure mechanical fatigue crack faces. *Highest priority*: this single test most directly discriminates (b) from (a)/(c)/(d)/(e) and also checks the falsification condition above (confirms the subsurface-origin reading).
2. **Used-oil analysis specifically bracketing the cold-snap period**: viscosity-at-temperature, moisture content, total acid number (TAN), and additive (ZDDP/anti-wear package) depletion. *Second priority*: directly tests (a) and (e), and directly tests whether the operator's viscosity claim has any factual basis at all (A-1 is currently unverified).
3. **Shaft/bearing common-mode voltage and grounding measurements** at the generator-end bearing, plus a check of converter switching characteristics (dv/dt, common-mode choke status if fitted). *Third priority, paired with #1*: directly tests (b), and is decisive for the insulated-bearing/grounding-brush spec question in §9.
4. **Inspect all other drivetrain bearings (LSS, intermediate-speed stage, HSS non-generator end) for fluting/frosting.** If fluting/frosting is present elsewhere but absent here, that argues *against* a turbine-wide electrical problem being the dominant driver of *this* bearing's failure specifically (or argues the generator-end bearing failed by a different/faster mechanism before fluting could develop elsewhere) — informative either way, and cheap to obtain since the gearbox is already open.
5. **Metallurgical inclusion-content/clean-steel verification** of the failed bearing against its original clean-steel specification (oxygen content, inclusion rating per ASTM E45/E1245 or equivalent), and a hardness/residual-stress traverse near the WEC zone. Tests (d)/(f) — whether substandard steel cleanliness or an anomalous heat-treatment condition contributed independently of hydrogen/electrical triggers.
6. **Pull SCADA/CM load-torque and rotor-speed history for the weeks preceding the kurtosis alarm**, specifically looking for light-load/variable-torque or grid-event periods coincident with or preceding the cold snap. Tests (c), and helps establish whether the "cold snap" the operator cited correlates with a torque-variability event rather than (or in addition to) a temperature/viscosity event.

Priority order reflects maximum discriminating power per unit of diagnostic effort: #1 and #3 can be run in parallel (not mutually dependent) and together are close to decisive on the electrical-vs-tribochemical question; #2 is cheap, likely already available or quickly obtainable from CM data, and directly checks the operator's own claim; #4–6 are confirmatory/exclusionary rather than primary.

---

## 9. Replacement Specification Recommendation

**What should change regardless of which upstream trigger is confirmed** (because the WEC-family diagnosis itself, HIGH confidence, already warrants this independent of §8's outcome):
- **Do not simply re-specify the original bearing at the original lubricant viscosity grade** — that directly treats the refuted hypothesis and would leave the actual WEC-susceptibility pathway unaddressed.
- **Upgrade to a bearing steel with a verified, tightened clean-steel/inclusion-content spec** (e.g., tighter oxygen-content and inclusion-rating limits than standard catalog bearings), since inclusion/carbide sites are the documented butterfly-nucleation points regardless of what triggers the hydrogen charging (GT-4, GT-7?). This is a no-regret change.
- **Switch to a lubricant additive package formulated/tested for reduced tribochemical hydrogen generation** (several current wind-gearbox-oil formulations are explicitly marketed against WEC risk) rather than simply specifying a higher base viscosity grade — matches the actual mechanism in §5(a)/(e), not the refuted mechanism in §4.
- **Tighten moisture-control practice** (breather/desiccant condition, oil sampling cadence) given the cold-snap/condensation plausibility in §5(e), independent of what §8 ultimately attributes as dominant.

**Conditional on §8's electrical-current findings:**
- **If #1 (SEM) or #3 (voltage/grounding) comes back positive for electrical discharge involvement:** specify an **insulated bearing (ceramic-coated or hybrid ceramic rolling elements) at the generator-end position**, and/or install/verify a **shaft-grounding brush and common-mode choke** on the generator feed. This is a materially different, additional spec change that should **not** be made preemptively without #1/#3 confirming it — hybrid/insulated bearings and grounding hardware carry their own cost and maintenance burden, and specifying them on the strength of position alone (GT-6) without morphological/electrical confirmation would be acting on the weakest-supported branch of §5 as if it were the strongest.

**What remains explicitly unresolved and flagged, not papered over:**
- Which of (a) tribochemical lubricant breakdown, (b) electrical bearing current, (c) transient micro-slip, or (e) moisture ingress is the *dominant* upstream trigger — current evidence supports (a)/(e) as most consistent with the morphology and the operator's own cold-snap observation, with (b) kept live specifically because of bearing position, but none is confirmed.
- Whether classical inclusion-content deficiency (d) is an independent contributing factor or coincidental — unresolved pending diagnostic #5.
- The precise mechanistic explanation for *why* WEC accelerates fatigue life by roughly an order of magnitude versus classical RCF — this is explicitly unresolved in the broader engineering literature (GT-10?), not just in this specific case, and the replacement spec decision should be made on the empirical/morphological evidence above, not on a claimed mechanistic certainty that the field itself does not yet have.

---

**Abandoned reasoning (ruled out, for the record):** (i) Pure boundary-lubrication wear-through (operator's hypothesis) — ruled out by C1, surface-vs-subsurface contact mechanics. (ii) Hard-particle contamination/dentation-initiated fatigue — no supporting debris finding in the given evidence; not pursued. (iii) Treating the 11%-of-L10 timing alone as proof of an anomalous mechanism — rejected as a standalone argument in §6 (Claim A); it only becomes meaningful evidence when combined with the independently-established morphological case (C1), which is how it's used in C2.

**Sources consulted (web search, summarized — not primary-source reads; this is why the corresponding ground truths above carry the `?` provenance flag):**
- [A study into the origins and significance of white etching cracks in bearing steels](https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/entities/publication/a1323269-2bf4-4d2d-822f-8a22970b8ded)
- [Elucidating the mechanisms of white etching crack failures within wind turbine gearbox bearings](https://udspace.udel.edu/items/b9b712bb-c23a-4cd2-bf34-c9c0e2f9af13/full)
- [lubesngreases.com — WEC overview](https://www.lubesngreases.com/?p=8065)
- [Stray currents can damage turbine bearings](https://www.power-eng.com/coal/stray-currents-can-damage-turbine-bearings/)
- [Electrical fluting bearing failure — Onyx Insight Failure Atlas](https://onyxinsight.com/resources-support/failure-atlas/electrical-fluting-bearing-failure/)
- [Analytical and experimental investigation of microstructural alterations in bearing steel in rolling contact fatigue (butterfly microstructure)](https://docs.lib.purdue.edu/dissertations/AAI10150086)
- [MDPI Lubricants — electrical fluting detail (TU Darmstadt)](https://tuprints.ulb.tu-darmstadt.de/27541/1/lubricants-12-00148-v3.pdf)

**Before authorizing the replacement spec:** run diagnostics #1–#3 above (SEM fractography, used-oil chemistry around the cold snap, shaft voltage/grounding) — these three are the minimum set needed to move the upstream-trigger confidence from MEDIUM to HIGH and to decide whether the insulated-bearing/grounding-brush change is warranted or would be an unsupported, costly overcorrection.
